policy_title: Introduce Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism and Green Finance Mandate
stated: Labour supports introducing a carbon border adjustment mechanism to protect British industries during decarbonisation and prevent lower-quality goods dumping. They will also mandate UK-regulated financial institutions and FTSE 100 companies to develop and implement credible transition plans aligned with the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C goal, making the UK a global green finance capital.

source.quote: British industry is also held back by high electricity costs, which has often made investing here uncompetitive. Labour’s clean energy mission will drive down those bills, making British businesses internationally competitive while our National Wealth Fund supports the most energy intensive sectors to decarbonise. Labour supports the introduction of a carbon border adjustment mechanism. This will protect British industries as we decarbonise, prevent countries from dumping lower-quality goods into British markets, and support the UK to meet our climate objectives. Labour will make the UK the green finance capital of the world, mandating UK-regulated financial institutions – including banks, asset managers, pension funds, and insurers – and FTSE 100 companies to develop and implement credible transition plans that align with the 1.5°C goal of the Paris Agreement.

bearing_set.reason: Both instruments directly target emissions trajectory: the CBAM prevents carbon leakage by pricing imports on embedded carbon, while the green finance mandate aligns capital allocation with the Paris 1.5°C pathway — together a material, contested effect on decarbonisation speed and credibility.

The CBAM is explicitly designed to protect energy-intensive British industries (e.g. steel, aluminium, cement) from lower-standard competition during decarbonisation, with direct plausible effects on employment levels and job quality in those sectors; the finance mandate could reshape capital flows toward or away from existing industrial workforces.

CBAM shapes UK industrial competitiveness and business investment during decarbonisation (near-term cost pressure on import-reliant downstream sectors vs. long-term protection of domestic producers); the green finance mandate explicitly targets capital allocation to make the UK a 'green finance capital', with real dual-horizon effects on productivity and economic opportunity.

membership_note: Two distinct mechanisms — a trade instrument and a financial regulation — justify three bearings: O6 as the primary target, O13 for the competitiveness and capital-allocation effects (dual-horizon), and O4 for the concrete job-security mechanism in exposed industries. Fiscal revenue from CBAM could bear on O12 but the policy does not specify the revenue-routing mechanism so the effect cannot be pinned to a specific indicator; left out accordingly.
